svg.title: How a switch with an older but higher VTP revision wipes VLANs from the whole domain, and the four modes that decide whether it can
svg.desc: Four steps in a chain. A spare switch returns to the network carrying revision forty two while the estate is at thirty eight, and older but higher wins. Its database is propagated everywhere. The database predates VLAN 20 and VLAN 99. Both disappear from every switch, their SVI interfaces go down, and voice and data fail together. A table beside it describes server, client, transparent and off modes, and a note says the only benefit is saving a few configuration lines, which configuration management already provides without the contagion.
svg.text: VTP is the only protocol in this chapter that can delete configuration you never touched
It resolves conflicts by revision number, not by truth — and a spare switch from the store room always wins
A spare switch returns, revision 42
the estate is at revision 38; the newcomer is older in configuration and higher in number
Higher revision wins the argument
every switch accepts the database from the highest revision, content never compared
Its database predates VLAN 20 and 99
those VLANs were added in the last two years, on a switch that has been powered off since
They disappear from every switch at once
voice and management VLANs deleted → SVIs down → phones and management both lost
no single device did anything wrong; the protocol did exactly what it was designed to do
Recovery is not a rollback: nothing was saved, and the database must be rebuilt by hand.
FOUR MODES
server
creates and deletes, and propagates what it holds
client
accepts everything, cannot create anything
transparent
forwards advertisements but keeps its own database
off
does not participate at all — the only safe default
The single benefit is saving a few lines of configuration
on every switch. Configuration management already does
that, without the contagion and without the revision race.
Cost of leaving it on: one unlabelled spare switch
and one afternoon of rebuilding every VLAN by hand.
The decision is not a judgement call: turn VTP off, everywhere, and if a mode must be kept for an inherited network, make it transparent rather than server.
If VTP must stay on, the only defence is discipline that no team sustains — every switch labelled with its revision, and nothing ever powered on without a wipe.
Compare the two risks honestly: VTP saves minutes per VLAN, and costs the whole estate once. That trade is settled before the meeting starts.
